case_study_insert.main_stem: Goldensheaf Milling Company (GSM) is a public limited company in the flour milling and baking-mix sector, employing a workforce of 260. Founded in 1988 by Arthur Bellingham, GSM is led by chief executive Duncan Pryce and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership and elected staff councils. The company plans to invest $1,500,000 in a new wholegrain flour and baking-mix production plant, financed by a $900,000 share issue and a $600,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $540,000 a year, a variable cost of $11.30 a unit and a selling price of $18.50, and currently produces 150,000 units a year. GSM faces two problems: spillage and dust waste is running at 4.8% of throughput, and the business faces a skills gap in certified mill operatives.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Milling Waste and Quality Report — Q3 2026: The mill produced 36,500 bags (25 kg) last quarter. Spillage and dust waste ran at 4.8% of throughput, up from 3.9% a year ago. Off-spec flour rejected at 1.2%. Complaints from wholesale bakery clients fell from 31 to 14 per month. Average delivery time is 3.8 days. A survey of 900 wholesale bakery buyers found that 57% would pay up to $0.75 more per bag for certified low-waste wholegrain flour, and 49% want ISO 22000 certification across suppliers; certified mill operatives remain scarce in the regional labour market, and on-site training with external assessors costs $1,100 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Goldensheaf Milling Company as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.25%, the fourth rise this year, increasing financing costs for the company's bank borrowings. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $13.32 to $14.17 per hour from April 2027, raising wage bills. (3) Wheat costs have risen 10.7% year-on-year, and food inflation is running at 7.6%, while consumer spending on home-baking ingredients grew 5.2% in the same period.

questions.question_text: GSM plans to fund the wholegrain plant partly with a $900,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for GSM of using the share issue instead of increasing the $600,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue brings in $900,000 without creating any repayment obligation or interest charge, so GSM's fixed costs do not rise on top of the existing $540,000 a year. This protects the profit margin and cash flow of a public company whose $1,500,000 plant must also bear a rising interest-rate environment, and keeps headroom with the bank for working capital such as wheat purchases amid 10.7% input inflation.

Point 2: Equity finance spreads ownership risk and strengthens the Statement of Financial Position for future negotiations with wholesale bakery clients and ISO 22000 auditors, since capital employed rises without extra debt. Dividend payments can be varied or passed in a difficult year, unlike loan interest, giving GSM flexibility through wheat-price cycles; and the share issue deepens the public shareholder base, potentially raising GSM's profile before it supplies national baking-mix contracts — and keeping the balance sheet clean at exactly the moment auditors will scrutinise the expansion funding.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Goldensheaf Milling Company and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: GSM is launching its certified low-waste wholegrain flour for wholesale bakeries. Consider exhibiting at the National Bakery Trade Exhibition, advertising in a baking-industry trade magazine, or running a LinkedIn business-to-business campaign. Which should GSM choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National Bakery Trade Exhibition: An exhibition stand would put GSM sales staff face to face with bakery purchasing managers, allow live sampling of the wholegrain blend, and generate warm leads within two days. The drawbacks are high one-off stand and staffing costs, limited to attendees over a single weekend, and no lasting presence; for a public company already financing a $1,500,000 plant, the cost per qualified lead is uncertain, and follow-up still has to be sold over weeks.

Baking-industry trade magazine advertising: A full-page feature in a leading baking title would reach thousands of bakery owners and production managers who read it for supplier news, building credibility for the certified low-waste claim backed by the 57% of 900 surveyed buyers willing to pay up to $0.75 more per bag. However, print frequency is monthly, response is passive and slow, and measuring return on spend requires reader-response mechanisms; coverage skews toward larger bakeries and misses smaller regional firms that GSM can profitably serve.

LinkedIn business-to-business campaign: Targeted LinkedIn adverts and Duncan Pryce's company-page content can reach bakery owners, production directors and procurement managers by job title, sector and region, showcase the 49% of buyers wanting ISO 22000 certification, link directly to a sample-request form, and deliver measurable click-through and cost-per-lead within weeks. It complements the trade exhibition's reach at a fraction of the cost, though it requires disciplined content and cannot replace human relationship-building with the largest national bakery accounts.

Recommendation: GSM should choose the LinkedIn business-to-business campaign. It is targeted precisely at the bakery procurement decision-makers across every region GSM delivers to (3.8 days), it is measurable in lead cost against the value of 150,000 units a year, it reinforces the ISO 22000 and low-waste certifications that 57% and 49% of surveyed buyers demand, and it scales with the new plant; the trade exhibition is rejected as a costly, one-weekend event with limited post-event conversion and no measurable pipeline, and the trade magazine is rejected as too passive and slow to support a 25 kg certified launch nationwide, though GSM should retain a modest magazine presence for brand authority.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of GSM with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of GSM with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the exhibition and magazine are rejected.

questions.question_text: GSM's skills gap in certified mill operatives is holding back the new wholegrain line. Explain two benefits for GSM of using democratic leadership with elected staff councils to close this skills gap.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership and staff councils give the 260 employees a formal voice in scheduling training, shift patterns and wholegrain-line procedures, so the best ideas for reducing the 4.8% spillage and dust waste come from the millers themselves. Staff who help design the new routines commit to them, which shortens the learning curve for certified operatives and protects off-spec rejection rates at 1.2% while the plant ramps up — exactly the certified-operative confidence wholesale bakery auditors will demand.

Point 2: Involving staff councils improves retention of experienced millers just when certified operatives are scarce in the regional labour market; employees who feel consulted stay longer, saving external recruitment fees and the $1,100 per employee assessor cost for training replacements. Consultation also surfaces health and safety concerns about dust and spillage early, reducing accident risk and waste simultaneously on the new line, and it gives Arthur Bellingham's founding values a living role in the modern 260-person company rather than a framed mission statement.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GSM's skills gap, waste levels and staff councils.

questions.question_text: GSM faces a skills gap on its new wholegrain line. Consider training its existing workforce with external assessors or recruiting certified mill operatives externally. Which should GSM choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Training existing workforce with external assessors: Developing current staff costs $1,100 per employee with external assessors certifying competencies; for a cohort of, say, 20 operatives that is $22,000 — modest against $1,500,000. Internal candidates already know GSM's hygiene culture, the 25 kg bagging line, and the ISO 22000 audit environment, so disruption is minimal, morale rises, and the elected staff councils can help schedule around production of 36,500 bags a quarter. Drawbacks are that some current staff may lack aptitude for the more technical wholegrain process, training takes time away from shifts, and assessed competency is individual, so a failed assessment wastes part of the $22,000.

Recruiting certified mill operatives externally: External hires bring immediate certified competence, fresh techniques from other mills and machinery experience from day one, ideal when the wholegrain line starts up and the 4.8% waste problem cannot wait. However, certified operatives are scarce regionally, salaries command a premium, induction into GSM's culture and ISO standards takes weeks, and poaching risks resentment among long-serving staff passed over for certification, undermining the democratic staff-council compact that keeps turnover low.

Decision: GSM should train its existing workforce with external assessors as the primary route, supplemented by recruiting two or three certified operatives externally as line leads and mentors. Training builds a home-grown certified cohort, preserves morale and process knowledge, and costs far less; pure external recruitment is rejected because the scarce regional talent could idle the new line at launch, add salary inflation, and weaken the internal pipeline GSM needs for ISO 22000 recertification — while recruiting only internally is rejected too, because line leads accelerate everyone's competence and bring outside best practice to the 1.2% off-spec target immediately.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two workforce options with limited application to GSM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of both options in the context of GSM's skills gap and expansion.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of GSM with a well-justified decision covering cost, scarcity, morale and certification.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how GSM's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $540,000 ÷ ($18.50 − $11.30) = $540,000 ÷ $7.20 = 75,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 75,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $18.50 − $11.30 = $7.20. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.20.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways GSM's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. GSM's managers can compare the 75,000-unit break-even output with actual production of 150,000 units to confirm the mill is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 75,000 units, which de-risks approving the $1,500,000 plant ahead of the next baking season.
2. Contribution per unit of $7.20 lets GSM model wheat-cost pass-through: if 10.7% wheat inflation forces a price rise to $18.95, contribution becomes $8.15, so managers can negotiate bakery contracts with evidence rather than guesswork.
3. Fixed costs of $540,000 and contribution per unit can be used to test the affordability of the $600,000 bank-loan element of the expansion, checking annual loan service against the 75,000-unit safety cushion before drawing the facility.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($540,000 ÷ 150,000 units + $11.30 = $14.90 a unit) to benchmark quarters, quantify the $ cost of 4.8% spillage waste and 1.2% off-spec flour, and target lean interventions in the wholegrain plant, where each saved kilogram of waste falls straight to the bottom line.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 75,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.20 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 75,000 units against 150,000-unit output; bakery-contract price modelling from $7.20 contribution; bank-loan affordability checks on the $600,000 element of the $1,500,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at $14.90 to attack the 4.8% spillage waste and 1.2% off-spec flour.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GSM's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Which judgement do the figures support — has GSM's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.43 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.53 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.89 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.00 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $260,000 inventories + $330,000 trade receivables + $95,000 cash = $685,000; 2025 current assets = $230,000 + $360,000 + $70,000 = $660,000. Short-term coverage 2024 = $685,000 ÷ $480,000 = 1.43; 2025 = $660,000 ÷ $430,000 = 1.53. Quick coverage excluding inventories 2024 = ($685,000 − $260,000) ÷ $480,000 = $425,000 ÷ $480,000 = 0.89; 2025 = ($660,000 − $230,000) ÷ $430,000 = $430,000 ÷ $430,000 = 1.00.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved, though with a cash caveat. The coverage of immediate obligations rose from 1.43 to 1.53, helped by current liabilities falling from $480,000 to $430,000, and the quick coverage improved from 0.89 to exactly 1.00, meaning GSM can now meet its short-term debts without selling a single bag of flour — significant while a $600,000 bank loan is attached to the $1,500,000 plant. However, cash fell from $95,000 to $70,000 even as receivables rose from $330,000 to $360,000, so bakery customers are paying more slowly and GSM is financing working capital from reduced cash headroom; if wholesale clients stretch to 60–90 day terms, the wholegrain launch could strain precisely when wheat purchases peak. Inventories fell prudently to $230,000, freeing working capital, but the company should watch for off-spec flour quarantine adding back stock unexpectedly.

Conclusion: GSM's financial position has improved, modestly. Both the current ratio (1.43 to 1.53) and the acid test ratio (0.89 to 1.00) show stronger short-term solvency, and the share issue rather than extra borrowing underpins the gain. The residual risks are the falling cash balance and rising receivables, so GSM should tighten wholesale credit terms, collect faster from the 57% premium-willing bakery segment, and refinance part of the bank loan as the new plant ramps up to protect the waste and off-spec recovery on the new line.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether GSM's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for GSM of introducing certified low-waste wholegrain flour production.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Certified low-waste wholegrain flour lets GSM capture the 57% of 900 surveyed bakery buyers willing to pay up to $0.75 more per bag, protecting and potentially lifting the $18.50 price toward the $19.25 premium. The 4.8% spillage and dust waste falling toward the off-spec rate would recover thousands of dollars of flour per quarter; and ISO 22000 or low-waste certification satisfies the 49% of buyers who want certified suppliers, helping win national baking-mix contracts that support the $1,500,000 wholegrain plant.

Disadvantage: Certification brings audit fees, record-keeping, segregated production runs and sometimes lower flour yields, raising the $11.30 variable cost and the $540,000 fixed-cost base while the process beds in. Any audit failure would remove the low-waste and ISO 22000 claims just as supermarket and bakery buyers are checking them, threatening listings and the $0.75 premium; and tighter quality windows can clash with the 1.2% off-spec rejection target, forcing more rework at a time when the line is already fighting 4.8% spillage and a certified-operative shortage.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GSM's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.7% rise in wheat costs will affect GSM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.25%): GSM carries a $600,000 bank loan attached to the $1,500,000 plant; on a variable or repricing facility a 0.50-point rise adds roughly $3,000 a year in interest, modest against $540,000 fixed costs and $18.50 pricing. Higher rates also raise any overdraft used for wheat purchases and can cool consumer home-baking spending if mortgages rise; for GSM the direct cash hit is small, though it raises the hurdle any further capital spending must clear and slightly tightens the credit outlook for wholesale bakery clients.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $14.17 per hour): GSM employs 260 staff; if most earn near the current $13.32 minimum, a 6.4% rise adds roughly $1,700 per worker, or about $440,000 a year across the full workforce — a major payroll pressure, though many mill operatives and engineers earn above minimum, so the true figure is somewhat lower. The rise lands exactly when the new plant needs to hit 1.2% off-spec flour targets and may squeeze discretionary training budgets, making productivity from the certified cohort essential to absorb it.

Wheat cost inflation (10.7% year-on-year): Wheat dominates the $11.30 variable cost. A 10.7% rise on the wheat component adds roughly $0.90–$1.10 per 25 kg bag; at 150,000 units that is about $135,000–$165,000 a year, cutting contribution from $7.20 toward $6.10–$6.30 before price rises, exactly as GSM launches flour off the new wholegrain plant and tries to hold $18.50 with a promised $0.75 premium for certified low-waste product.

Conclusion: The 10.7% rise in wheat costs will have the greatest impact. It is the largest single raw material cost, it compounds with every unit milled — roughly $135,000–$165,000 a year at current volumes and far more once the plant ramps — and it attacks the contribution margin that funds the $600,000 bank loan. The minimum-wage increase is the second-biggest pressure and can be mitigated through automation on the new line and through democratic staff councils raising labour productivity, while the interest-rate rise is the smallest in cash terms at a few thousand dollars and can be capped by fixing loan pricing; GSM should nevertheless hedge wheat purchases and renegotiate wholesale bakery contracts to pass through part of the cost before the April 2027 wage change compounds it.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to GSM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on GSM's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of GSM with a well-justified judgement that wheat-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
